claim: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the second most-common cause for the prescription of antibiotics.
source: Urinary tract infections (UTIs), the second most-common cause for the prescription of antibiotics (Foxman, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Foxman, 2010

claim: Recurrence of UTIs occurs in about 25% of all UTIs.
source: Recurrence occurs in about 25% of all UTIs (Foxman et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Foxman et al., 2000

claim: More than 60% of women are diagnosed with a UTI at least once in their lifetime.
source: more than 60% of women are diagnosed with a UTI at least once in their lifetime (Klein and Hultgren, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein and Hultgren, 2020

claim: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the causative agent for the majority of UTIs.
source: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), the causative agent for the majority of UTIs
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus

claim: Much of our current understanding of early stages of UTI and the intracellular lifestyle is derived from studies in the mouse model.
source: Much of our current understanding of early stages of UTI and the intracellular lifestyle is derived from studies in the mouse model (Anderson, 2003; Duraiswamy et al., 2018; Hannan et al., 2012; Hung et al., 2009; Justice et al., 2004; Schwartz et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to mouse model studies

claim: Intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) are composed of thousands of bacteria within individual superficial bladder cells.
source: Examinations of mouse bladder explants via microscopy have revealed the formation of intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) composed of thousands of bacteria within individual superficial bladder cells (Justice et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Justice et al., 2004

claim: IBCs have been harvested from the urine of cystitis patients.
source: IBCs also play a prominent role in clinical infection and have also been harvested from the urine of cystitis patients (Robino et al., 2013; Rosen et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Robino et al., 2013 and Rosen et al., 2007

claim: IBCs have a linear progression from an early stage of colonization by single bacteria to an intermediate stage of biofilm-like communities culminating in the release of bacteria at the late stage.
source: These structures are considered to have a linear progression from an early stage of colonization by single bacteria to an intermediate stage of biofilm-like communities culminating in the release of bacteria at the late stage (Anderson, 2003; Justice et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson, 2003 and Justice et al., 2004

claim: The bladder-chip model enables co-culture of bladder epithelial cells and bladder microvascular endothelial cells.
source: We established a bladder-chip infection model by co-culturing HMVEC-Bd primary human bladder microvascular endothelial cells with the 5637 human bladder epithelial cell line (HTB-9, epithelial cells) in a novel bladder-chip approach (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental description and Figure 1A showing the co-culture setup

claim: Epithelial cells in the bladder-chip express high levels of EpCAM.
source: Immunostaining verified that the epithelial and endothelial cells formed confluent monolayers (cell densities in Table 1) with high expression of junction markers such as epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM) in the epithelial cell layer
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data described in the text

claim: Endothelial cells in the bladder-chip express PECAM-1 and VE-cadherin.
source: platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1) and VE-cadherin in the endothelial cell layer (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–H)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and figures showing expression

claim: A majority of the epithelial cells expressed cytokeratin 7 (CK7), a general uroepithelial marker.
source: Similarly, a majority of the epithelial cells expressed cytokeratin 7 (CK7), a general uroepithelial marker
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data described in the text

claim: A majority of the epithelial cells expressed cytokeratin 8 (CK8), a differentiated uroepithelial marker.
source: and cytokeratin 8 (CK8), a differentiated uroepithelial marker both in monoculture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I,J) and on-chip (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and figures

claim: The 5637 cells showed high expression of uroplakin-3a (UP3a).
source: A total of 5637 cells showed high expression of uroplakin-3a (UP3a) which has been shown to be essential for UPEC infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K; Martinez et al., 2000; Mulvey et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and figure, with citations to Martinez et al., 2000 and Mulvey et al., 1998

claim: Uroplakin-3a is essential for UPEC infection.
source: uroplakin-3a (UP3a) which has been shown to be essential for UPEC infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K; Martinez et al., 2000; Mulvey et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2000 and Mulvey et al., 1998

claim: Only a small proportion of 5637 epithelial cells were positive for the basal cell marker cytokeratin 1 (CK1).
source: but only a small proportion of epithelial cells were positive for the basal cell marker cytokeratin 1 (CK1), in agreement with the umbrella cell nature of the 5637 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2L,M; Duncan et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and figures, with citations to Duncan et al., 2004 and Smith et al., 2006

claim: The bladder-chip enables the flow of media with different compositions through the epithelial and vascular channels.
source: the chip design enables the flow of media with different compositions through the epithelial and vascular channels. We used this feature to mimic bladder physiology by perfusion of diluted pooled human urine on the epithelial side and endothelial cell medium on the vascular side
evidence: Supported by experimental description

claim: A maximum strain of 90% and 130% can be applied to bladder explants in the circumferential and longitudinal directions in ex vivo studies in rat bladders.
source: Ex vivo studies in rat bladders report that a maximum strain of 90% and 130% can be applied to bladder explants in the circumferential and longitudinal directions (Gloeckner et al., 2002; Parekh et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gloeckner et al., 2002 and Parekh et al., 2010

claim: A linear strain of 0% to 19% was achieved by application of negative pressure (0 to −900 mbar) in the bladder-chip.
source: A plot of applied pressure vs. strain was linear, and we achieved a dynamic range of linear strain (0% to 19%) by application of negative pressure (0 to −900 mbar)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements described in the text

claim: The bladder-chip model applies a maximum linear strain of 10% to mimic bladder filling and voiding.
source: We therefore limited the linear strain applied to a maximum of 10%, which is of the same order of magnitude, albeit a small fraction of the typical strain experienced by the bladder tissue in vivo
evidence: Supported by experimental description

claim: The bladder filling and voiding cycle was modeled over a 6 hr duty cycle.
source: We then modeled the bladder filling and voiding over a 6 hr duty cycle with different states: filling bladder (0 to 2 hr, 0% to 10% strain), filled bladder (2 to 4 hr, 10% strain), voiding bladder over a period of 2 min (4 hr to 4:02 hr, 10% to 0% strain), and voided bladder (4:02 hr to 6 hr, 0% strain) (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental description and Figure 1D

claim: UPEC attachment and invasion of bladder epithelial cells is sensitive to fluidic shear stress.
source: UPEC attachment and invasion of bladder epithelial cells has been shown to be sensitive to fluidic shear stress (Andersen et al., 2012; Zalewska-Piątek et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Andersen et al., 2012 and Zalewska-Piątek et al., 2020

claim: Low shear stress conditions enhance bacterial adhesion to epithelial cells.
source: Low shear stress conditions have been recently reported to enhance bacterial adhesion to epithelial cells (Zalewska-Piątek et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zalewska-Piątek et al., 2020

claim: The epithelial layer was infected under a flow rate of 1.2 ml/hr corresponding to a shear stress of 0.02 dyne cm−2.
source: we infected the epithelial layer on the bladder-chip under a flow rate of 1.2 ml/hr (corresponding to a shear stress of 0.02 dyne cm−2) for a period of 1.5–2 hr
evidence: Supported by experimental description

claim: The typical infectious dose at the end of the infection period was low (<one bacterium per epithelial cell).

evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Neutrophils are the first line of defense in UTIs.
source: Among innate immune cells, neutrophils are the first line of defense in UTIs (Haraoka et al., 1999)

evidence: Supported by experimental description and citation to Hsieh et al., 2007
